The power is thin right now, four home runs and a .13 ISO at A, and the translated .104 ISO lands well short of where MLB hitters average out, so if the bat speed doesn't grow into game power as he fills out, the walk rate becomes a nice feature on a limited profile rather than the foundation of something. Thirty stolen bases at A tell you the speed is usable and adds a dimension the bat alone doesn't yet provide. If the bat and speed develop together, he profiles as more than bench depth; if the ISO stays flat, a patient, fast fourth outfielder is roughly what's left.

828318_hitter.text: The contact-and-walk combination at A ball is genuinely strange for a 19-year-old: 11 strikeouts against 22 walks in 126 plate appearances, a 9 K% that translates to 18% against MLB competition, where most hitters swing and miss far more often. What it doesn't yet come with is power, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .119 trails a league where the average hitter is at .150 — meaning Lo Re needs the bat-to-ball and plate patience to carry him if the gap power never arrives. If it develops over the next two to three years, you're looking at a low-end everyday second baseman; if the profile stays contact-and-speed without the pop growing, the ceiling compresses to a bench piece who can work a count.

828335_hitter.text: The .225 ISO at AA is the loudest thing here, and the translation suggests it carries — a projected .162 ISO at the MLB level would sit above the league average, which means the raw power has a legitimate major-league shape. That gap is the whole problem, because command without swing-and-miss at 19 leaves a 1.4 WHIP and a 5.0 ERA, and the projection floor and ceiling land in the same place — a depth arm if the bat-missing never arrives, something slightly more useful if it does, though ValuCast puts only a 6% handle on the latter. The read hinges entirely on whether the strikeout stuff develops in the next level or two; without it, the command grades out as fringy survival skill rather than a real carrying tool.

828557_hitter.text: Blaine Bullard is a 19-year-old center fielder swinging and missing at a high rate without offsetting walk discipline—the 27.6% strikeout rate ranks in the 34th percentile, and his 7.3% walk rate is well below league average. The sample is active and live (246 PA as of mid-June), but his current shape—high strikeouts, low walks, moderate power—projects as a long-term platoon bat or bench piece at best.

828667_hitter.text: Sixteen home runs and 56 walks in 343 plate appearances at A ball — that's a discipline profile scouts don't usually see this young. The translation is the honest hang-up: that 26% strikeout rate tightens to 30% against MLB-caliber arms, and the ISO compresses to .141 while the average MLB hitter sits at .150, giving back most of the power advantage. If the discipline holds as competition improves but the swing-and-miss doesn't shrink, you're looking at a low-end everyday right fielder; if the strikeouts metastasize, what's left is a reserve with a good eye.

828672_pitcher.text: Jagger Beck is a 19-year-old right-hander generating swing-and-miss at a strong rate—11.7 K/9 ranks 80th percentile in the ValuCast pitcher pool—while maintaining excellent K-BB% (21.6%, 90th percentile) through tight walk control at 3.6 BB/9. The chief risk is that MLB translation downgrades his strikeout rate meaningfully to 8.2 K/9, closing the skill gap between him and average, while his walk rate ticks up to 3.9 BB/9 in the majors. This is a 40-inning sample in active play, so the read reflects early-season feel without the depth of conviction that comes with volume.

828685_hitter.text: The walk rate is the argument here. The swing-and-contact side is softer: his 22% strikeout rate at A ticks up to 25.7% against MLB pitching, which erases some of the plate-discipline gains, and the MLB-equivalent ISO of .132 falls short of where a first baseman needs to be if strikeouts are climbing too. If the eye holds and the bat catches up as an 18-year-old, a low-end everyday regular is the ceiling; if the strikeouts bleed up and the power stalls, the profile thins to reserve.

828824_hitter.text: The .461 OBP sits at the 99th percentile of his hitter pool, and the 18% walk rate translates to a projected 12.5% at the big-league level, well clear of the 8.5% MLB average. 829033_hitter.text: The walk rate is the loudest thing on this card. The problem is everything else: three home runs, a .084 ISO, and a slugging percentile sitting at 24th among peers, and an MLB-equivalent ISO of .087 when the big-league average is .150 says the translation doesn't fix the gap. If some power emerges by the upper minors, the approach gives him a real foundation; if it doesn't, a .386 OBP built on walks with a .341 SLG is a bench piece at best.

829052_hitter.text: Breyson Guedez is a young left-handed hitter working through strikeout noise at the A level, flashing contact ability (.282 avg, 83rd percentile) but generating minimal power (.119 ISO, 31st percentile) and very little leverage on base (6.6% BB rate, 8th percentile). The sample is current and meaningful, but at 18 with moderate command and modest thump so far, this looks like a years-away organizational depth profile rather than a near-term contributor.

829210_hitter.text: Ty Harvey is a 19-year-old catcher showing early discipline at the plate—19% BB% on a 58 PA sample—but swinging and missing at a concerning clip (24.1% K%).
